title: San Acacio Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: San Acacio wells have a 170-foot median depth and typical finished costs of $14,500-$24,800.
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near San Acacio means understanding what nearby wells actually produce, not relying on a generic Colorado estimate. Records within 5 miles show 255 permitted wells, with 142 recorded as constructed. Of those, 148 report total depth, 53 report pump yield, and 24 report static water level.

The local record points to moderate drilling depths and generally usable yields, but the water-level measurements deserve attention. Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with some wells in the Unconfined San Luis Valley Aquifer. Neighboring wells are useful evidence, but they do not guarantee the result on a new lot.

sections.heading: San Acacio well depths and the ground below
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near San Acacio is 170 feet. The middle half runs from 117 to 280 feet, so a typical drilling bid should not be based on the median alone. A contractor may encounter a shallower hole near the low end or need to drill substantially farther near the high end.

Most wells, 61%, fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 22% are between 300 and 600 feet, while the deepest record reaches 850 feet. The ground is described as mixed sedimentary and alluvial material. Permits most often name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, where water-bearing fractures can vary sharply from one location to the next. Casing, grout, and the final pump setup should be specified in the driller's proposal.

sections.heading: What San Acacio wells produce
sections.html:
Among the 53 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half spans 10.0 to 60.0 gallons per minute, which is a wide spread and a reminder that nearby wells can perform very differently.

The recorded mix is encouraging for ordinary household planning: 51% report more than 15 gallons per minute, and 45% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Four percent report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while none are recorded under 1 gallon per minute. These are reported well yields, not a promise of continuous household supply. Ask for the completion report and a sustained yield test. An exempt household-use well still has a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit, and additional water rights may require an augmentation plan in an over-appropriated basin.

sections.heading: Water levels near San Acacio over time
sections.html:
The reported static water level has a median depth of 100 feet below the surface. The middle half is 48 to 140 feet, giving a useful range for planning pump depth, trenching, and storage equipment.

The decade figures show a change worth investigating: the median measured water level was 64 feet below ground in the 2010s and 117 feet in the 2020s. That pattern is consistent with deeper measured water levels in the newer decade, but only 24 wells report static water levels, and the measurements may come from different locations, aquifers, seasons, and conditions. It is not enough by itself to prove a regional decline. For a purchase, compare the closest completed wells and request current measurements when possible.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers serving the area
sections.html:
San Acacio has a long permit record rather than a short burst of recent construction. The records show 3 permits in the 1950s, 6 in the 1960s, 28 in the 1970s, 14 in the 1980s, 38 in the 1990s, 24 in the 2000s, 45 in the 2010s, and 28 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

Heersink Drilling, listed as Heersink, Scott, appears most often with 22 records. Olsen, Gayln F. appears on 15, and Mitchell Drilling Co., listed as Mitchell Jr., John C., appears on 9. These names show who has worked in the mapped record; they are not a recommendation. Before hiring, confirm current licensing, insurance, availability, the proposed construction method, and how the contractor handles an unsuccessful hole.

sections.heading: What a new well costs near San Acacio
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground described here, the cost model uses $50 to $75 per drilled foot. At the 170-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $8,500 to $12,800. This is the hole only, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $14,500 to $24,800 at the median depth. The 117-to-280-foot middle range explains why bids can differ substantially between nearby lots. Get the price in writing, including casing, grout, drilling through difficult material, water testing, abandonment of a dry hole, power distance, trench restoration, and any permit or engineering work. A deeper-than-median hole can move the total beyond the typical finished range.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only concern. The area has one mapped PFAS sampling or contamination site within about 10 miles and 15 historic mine features. There are no mapped EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those records do not establish the condition of a particular well, but they are reasons to check the exact parcel and test the water rather than assuming it is safe.

Ask for bacteria, nitrate, and other testing appropriate to the site, along with any available treatment history. Locate the septic system and proposed replacement area before finalizing a building plan. Septic setbacks, access for a drill rig, electrical service, trench routes, and the location of the wellhead all affect cost and feasibility. Fractured-bedrock conditions also make dry or weak holes harder to predict than the neighborhood median suggests.

sections.heading: Buying land near San Acacio: a practical plan
sections.html:
Start with the closest neighboring completion reports, not an average from the entire five-mile area. San Luis is about 8 miles away; Blanca is 16 miles, Fort Garland 17 miles, Sanford 19 miles, Manassa 21 miles, and La Jara 22 miles. Those places provide regional context, but the closest wells usually tell you more about the lot's ground and aquifer.

Before closing, confirm the DWR permit status and allowed use, inspect any existing pump and pressure equipment, and obtain a current water test. If building, have a driller and excavator review rig access, the well location, septic layout, power, and driveway grades together. Budget for a range around the local depth and yield data, and make the contract address what happens if the first hole does not produce enough water.

faq.q: How deep are wells in San Acacio, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth within 5 miles of San Acacio is 170 feet. The middle half runs from 117 to 280 feet. Most recorded wells are between 100 and 300 feet, but 22% fall between 300 and 600 feet and the deepest record is 850 feet. A nearby completion report is more useful than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in San Acacio?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 170-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $8,500 to $12,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $14,500 to $24,800. A deeper hole, difficult ground, long power run, or challenging access can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in San Acacio?
faq.a: Among 53 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0 to 60.0 gallons per minute. Fifty-one percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. These figures describe reported wells, not a guarantee for a new lot, so request a completion report and yield test.

faq.q: Is well water safe in San Acacio?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from the permit map alone. There is one mapped PFAS sampling or contamination site and 15 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with no mapped EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well, especially for bacteria, nitrate, and contaminants relevant to the parcel's history, and review any existing treatment records.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near San Acacio?
faq.a: The available measurements show deeper reported water levels in the newer decade: the median was 64 feet below surface in the 2010s and 117 feet in the 2020s. However, only 24 wells report static water levels, and locations, aquifers, seasons, and measurement conditions differ. The pattern deserves investigation but does not alone prove a regional decline.
